color/color: A color photo stores three numbers for every pixel: how much red, how much green, and how much blue. So it is three grids of numbers, stacked.
color/channel: Each grid is called a channel, like the left and right channels of stereo sound: separate streams, side by side.
color/edge: Now look for where a red apple meets green leaves. In the red channel, the apple is bright and the leaves are dark. In the green channel, it is the other way round.
color/flat: A flat filter on the red channel alone sees an edge, but it cannot tell red against green from red against black: in the red channel, the two look the same.
color/deep: So a filter reaches through every channel: a three by three patch in each, a block three deep, with twenty seven weights in all.
color/one: At each position it multiplies all twenty seven pairs and adds them up, into one number. Not one per color: one.
color/map: Slid to every position, those numbers fill one map, a single output channel: where the image looks like the filter, in all three colors at once.
many/shape: PyTorch, a Python library for neural networks, writes this image's shape channels first: three by thirty two by thirty two, for channels, height and width.
many/fit: A three wide filter that stays inside fits thirty two minus three plus one places across: thirty. The same goes down, so the map is thirty by thirty.
many/k: But one filter looks for one pattern. To find edges at other angles, or other colors, a layer has many filters, K of them, each with its own weights. Here, eight.
many/stack: Each filter makes its own map, and the maps stack up as the output's channels. Eight filters, eight channels: eight by thirty by thirty.
many/depth: So the input's depth sets how deep each filter is, and the number of filters sets how deep the output is.
many/alexnet: In 2012, AlexNet, from Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, opened with ninety six filters, each eleven by eleven by three. Its first layer turned three color channels into ninety six.
many/next: The next layer sees an input eight channels deep, so each of its filters is eight deep: eight by three by three, depth first.
layer/args: In PyTorch, a layer is built like this: n n dot conv two d, of three, eight, kernel size five. Three channels in; eight channels out, so eight filters; each five by five across. Kernel is another word for filter.
layer/weight: Each filter is then three deep: three by five by five. PyTorch keeps all eight in one array, filters first: eight, three, five, five. The out channels come first, then the in channels.
layer/out: On a three by thirty two by thirty two image, each filter fits thirty two minus five plus one places, twenty eight, down and across. So the output is eight by twenty eight by twenty eight.
